prompt:
Let $f:[1,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be a non-increasing function such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(2^{n+1})}{f(2^n)}<\frac12 .$$
Prove that
$$\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx<\infty .$$
answer: On $[2^n,2^{n+1}]$, $\int f\le2^nf(2^n)$, and $\sum 2^nf(2^n)$ converges by the ratio test because $\limsup\frac{2^{n+1}f(2^{n+1})}{2^nf(2^n)}<1$.

solutions.title: Dyadic blocks and the ratio test
solutions.body:
A monotone function is Riemann integrable on bounded intervals. Since $f$ is non-increasing and positive, on each dyadic block
$$0<\int_{2^n}^{2^{n+1}}f(x)\,dx\le(2^{n+1}-2^n)f(2^n)=2^nf(2^n)=:u_n .$$
The $u_n$ are positive and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}=2\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(2^{n+1})}{f(2^n)}<1,$$
so $\sum_n u_n<\infty$ by the ratio test. Hence for every $X\ge1$, choosing $N$ with $2^{N+1}\ge X$,
$$\int_1^Xf\le\sum_{n=0}^{N}\int_{2^n}^{2^{n+1}}f\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty u_n<\infty .$$
The integral $\int_1^X f$ is increasing in $X$ and bounded, so $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx$ converges. ∎

(Equivalently: by Cauchy condensation $\sum f(n)$ converges, and then the integral test gives the claim.)

prompt:
Let $M$ be the (tridiagonal) $10\times10$ matrix
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}
-1&3&0&0&\cdots&0&0\\
3&2&-1&0&\cdots&0&0\\
0&-1&2&-1&\cdots&0&0\\
\vdots&&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&&\vdots\\
0&0&\cdots&-1&2&-1&0\\
0&0&\cdots&0&-1&2&-1\\
0&0&\cdots&0&0&-1&2
\end{pmatrix}$$
(that is, $m_{11}=-1$, $m_{12}=m_{21}=3$, $m_{ii}=2$ for $2\le i\le10$, $m_{i,i+1}=m_{i+1,i}=-1$ for $2\le i\le9$, and all other entries $0$). Show that $M$ has exactly nine positive real eigenvalues (counted with multiplicities).
answer: $M$ is symmetric; on the 9-dimensional subspace $\{x_1=0\}$ the form $x^TMx=x_2^2+\sum(x_{i+1}-x_i)^2+x_{10}^2$ is positive definite, while $y=(1,-1,0,\dots,0)$ gives $y^TMy=-5<0$; a dimension count then gives exactly one negative and nine positive eigenvalues.

solutions.title: Quadratic form on a hyperplane
solutions.body:
$M$ is real symmetric, so it has $10$ real eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_{10}$ (with multiplicity) and an orthonormal eigenbasis.

**Positive on a 9-dimensional subspace.** Let $V_1=\{x\in\mathbb R^{10}:x_1=0\}$, $\dim V_1=9$. For $x=(0,x_2,\dots,x_{10})$, only the lower-right $9\times9$ block (2 on the diagonal, $-1$ next to it) matters:
$$x^TMx=2\sum_{i=2}^{10}x_i^2-2\sum_{i=2}^{9}x_ix_{i+1}=x_2^2+\sum_{i=2}^{9}(x_{i+1}-x_i)^2+x_{10}^2 .$$
This is $\ge0$, and $=0$ only if $x_2=0$, $x_3=x_2$, …, i.e. $x=0$. So $x^TMx>0$ for all $0\ne x\in V_1$.

**At most one non-positive eigenvalue.** Suppose $\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le0$, with orthonormal eigenvectors $y_1,y_2$. On $V_2=\operatorname{span}(y_1,y_2)$, for $y=\alpha_1y_1+\alpha_2y_2$,
$$y^TMy=\lambda_1\alpha_1^2+\lambda_2\alpha_2^2\le0 .$$
But $\dim V_1+\dim V_2=11>10$, so there is $0\ne y\in V_1\cap V_2$, for which $y^TMy>0$ and $y^TMy\le0$ — contradiction. Hence $\lambda_2>0$.

**At least one negative eigenvalue.** For $y=(1,-1,0,\dots,0)$,
$$y^TMy=m_{11}-2m_{12}+m_{22}=-1-6+2=-5<0 .$$
Writing $y$ in the eigenbasis, $y^TMy=\sum\lambda_i c_i^2$, so some $\lambda_i<0$; thus $\lambda_1<0$.

Therefore $\lambda_1<0<\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_{10}$: exactly nine eigenvalues are positive. ∎

solutions.title: Cauchy interlacing
solutions.body:
Delete the first row and column of $M$: the remaining $9\times9$ matrix $T$ is the tridiagonal matrix with $2$ on the diagonal and $-1$ beside it. As in the first solution, $x^TTx=x_1^2+\sum_{i=1}^{8}(x_{i+1}-x_i)^2+x_9^2>0$ for $x\ne0$, so all eigenvalues $\mu_1\le\dots\le\mu_9$ of $T$ are positive. (Explicitly $\mu_j=2-2\cos\frac{j\pi}{10}$.)

By the Cauchy interlacing theorem for the principal submatrix $T$ of the symmetric matrix $M$,
$$\lambda_1\le\mu_1\le\lambda_2\le\mu_2\le\dots\le\mu_9\le\lambda_{10},$$
so $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_{10}\ge\mu_1>0$. Finally $\lambda_1<0$: indeed $\lambda_1=\min_{\|y\|=1}y^TMy$ and $y=(1,-1,0,\dots,0)$ gives $y^TMy=-5<0$. Hence exactly nine eigenvalues are positive. ∎

prompt: Let $(A,+,\cdot)$ be a ring with unity, having the following property: for all $x\in A$ either $x^2=1$ or $x^n=0$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$. Show that $A$ is a commutative ring.
answer: Units satisfy $x^2=1$, so the unit group is commutative ($(xy)^2=1\Rightarrow xy=yx$); non-units are nilpotent, so $1-x$ is a unit for every non-unit $x$; then $xy=yx$ follows by replacing non-units $x$ by the units $1-x$.

solutions.title: Units commute, and $1-x$ is a unit for non-units
solutions.body:
If $1=0$, then $A=\{0\}$ is commutative; assume $1\ne0$. Let $U$ be the group of units.

**Units satisfy $x^2=1$.** A unit cannot be nilpotent (if $x^n=0$ with $x$ invertible, then $1=x^{-n}x^n=0$). So every unit satisfies $x^2=1$. Conversely, an element with $x^2=1$ is a unit. Hence $x\in U\iff x^2=1$, and every non-unit is nilpotent.

**$U$ is commutative.** For $x,y\in U$, $xy\in U$, so $xyxy=1$. Multiply by $x$ on the left and $y$ on the right and use $x^2=y^2=1$: $yx=x(xyxy)y=xy$.

**$1-x$ is a unit if $x$ is not.** A non-unit $x$ is nilpotent, $x^n=0$, and
$$(1-x)(1+x+\dots+x^{n-1})=1-x^n=1=(1+x+\dots+x^{n-1})(1-x) .$$

**Commutativity.** Let $x,y\in A$. For each of them, either it is a unit or $1-(\text{it})$ is; put $x'=x$ if $x\in U$, else $x'=1-x$, and similarly $y'$. Then $x',y'\in U$ commute. Since $x=x'$ or $x=1-x'$ (and $1$ commutes with everything), $x$ is a polynomial expression in $x'$ of the form $\pm x'+\text{const}$; likewise $y$ in $y'$. Expanding, $xy=yx$. For instance, if $x,y\notin U$:
$$(1-x)(1-y)=(1-y)(1-x)\iff1-x-y+xy=1-y-x+yx\iff xy=yx .$$
Hence $A$ is commutative. ∎

prompt:
Let $a,b,c,x,y,z,t$ be positive real numbers with $1\le x,y,z\le4$. Prove that
$$\frac{x}{(2a)^t}+\frac{y}{(2b)^t}+\frac{z}{(2c)^t}\ \ge\ \frac{y+z-x}{(b+c)^t}+\frac{z+x-y}{(c+a)^t}+\frac{x+y-z}{(a+b)^t} .$$
answer: A weighted Schur inequality $x(A-B)(A-C)+y(B-A)(B-C)+z(C-A)(C-B)\ge0$ (valid for weights in $[1,4]$), applied to $A=e^{-as},B=e^{-bs},C=e^{-cs}$ and integrated against $s^{t-1}ds$, using $\int_0^\infty s^{t-1}e^{-ps}ds=\Gamma(t)p^{-t}$.

solutions.title: Weighted Schur inequality plus a Gamma-integral
solutions.body:
**Lemma 1 (weighted Schur).** If $1\le x,y,z\le4$, then for all real $A,B,C$
$$x(A-B)(A-C)+y(B-A)(B-C)+z(C-A)(C-B)\ge0 .$$
*Proof.* The expression is symmetric under permuting $(A,x),(B,y),(C,z)$ simultaneously, and the hypothesis on the weights is symmetric, so assume $A\le B\le C$. With $U=B-A\ge0$, $V=C-B\ge0$ the expression equals
$$xU(U+V)-yUV+z(U+V)V\ \ge\ U(U+V)-4UV+(U+V)V=(U-V)^2\ge0,$$
using $x,z\ge1$, $y\le4$ and $U(U+V),\,UV,\,(U+V)V\ge0$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** For $p>0$ and $t>0$: $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty s^{t-1}e^{-ps}\,ds=\frac{\Gamma(t)}{p^t}$ (substitute $u=ps$).

**Proof of the inequality.** Apply Lemma 1 with $A=e^{-as}$, $B=e^{-bs}$, $C=e^{-cs}$ for each $s>0$. Expanding,
$$x(A-B)(A-C)+y(B-A)(B-C)+z(C-A)(C-B)=xA^2+yB^2+zC^2-(y+z-x)BC-(z+x-y)CA-(x+y-z)AB$$
(e.g. the coefficient of $BC$ is $x-y-z$). So for every $s>0$,
$$0\le xe^{-2as}+ye^{-2bs}+ze^{-2cs}-(y+z-x)e^{-(b+c)s}-(z+x-y)e^{-(c+a)s}-(x+y-z)e^{-(a+b)s}.$$
Multiply by $s^{t-1}$ and integrate over $(0,\infty)$ (every term is integrable by Lemma 2). Lemma 2 gives
$$0\le\Gamma(t)\left[\frac{x}{(2a)^t}+\frac{y}{(2b)^t}+\frac{z}{(2c)^t}-\frac{y+z-x}{(b+c)^t}-\frac{z+x-y}{(c+a)^t}-\frac{x+y-z}{(a+b)^t}\right].$$
Since $\Gamma(t)>0$, the claimed inequality follows. ∎
